summary.text: For \(n=550172\), an explicit prime count gives \(p_n<2^{23}\), while period \(29400\) modulo \(n\), a restriction to three index classes modulo \(588\), and a finite scan show that the residue \(63945\) is never attained for \(k<2^{24}\). A Chinese-remainder construction shows every residue is eventually attained, so \(a(n)\ge 2^{24}>2(p_n-1)\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 f(k)=2^k-k
\]
and let \(a(n)\) be the least positive integer \(m\) for which the values
\(f(1),\ldots,f(m)\) represent every residue class modulo \(n\). We disprove the conjectured inequality
\[
 a(n)<2(p_n-1)
\]
by taking
\[
 N=550172=4\cdot 7^3\cdot401
\]
and exhibiting the residue
\[
 R=63945
\]
which does not occur among the \(f(k)\) for \(1\leq k<2^{24}\). We will also show that \(p_{550172}<2^{23}\). If the conjecture held at \(N\), these two facts would be incompatible.

We first record the elementary periodicity principle used below. Suppose that
\[
 a^{s+D}\equiv a^s\pmod n.
\]
Multiplying this congruence by \(a^j\) gives the same assertion with \(s\) replaced by \(s+j\). Repeating it \(q\) times gives, for all nonnegative \(j,q\),
\[
 a^{s+j+Dq}\equiv a^{s+j}\pmod n. \tag{1}
\]
This does not require \(a\) to be invertible modulo \(n\).

For the present modulus, direct repeated-squaring computations give
\[
 2^{2+29400}\equiv2^2\pmod{550172}, \tag{2}
\]
and
\[
 2^{2+588}\equiv2^2\pmod{196}. \tag{3}
\]
These calculations can be made entirely with residues smaller than the respective moduli: successively square the current residue, reducing after every multiplication, and multiply the residues corresponding to the nonzero binary digits of the exponent. Thus (1), applied to (2), says
\[
 2^{2+j+29400q}\equiv2^{2+j}\pmod N, \tag{4}
\]
and its application to (3) gives the analogous period \(588\) modulo \(196\).

We now prove the missing-residue assertion. Suppose, for contradiction, that
\[
 1\leq k<2^{24}=16777216,
 \qquad 2^k-k\equiv63945\pmod N. \tag{5}
\]
The case \(k=1\) is immediately impossible, since \(2^1-1=1\not\equiv63945\pmod N\). Hence \(k\geq2\).

Since \(196\mid N\) and \(63945\equiv49\pmod{196}\), (5) implies
\[
 2^k-k\equiv49\pmod{196}. \tag{6}
\]
Put
\[
 t\equiv k-2\pmod{588},\qquad 0\leq t<588.
\]
By (3) and the periodicity principle,
\[
 2^k-k\equiv 2^{t+2}-(t+2)\pmod{196}.
\]
A finite calculation for \(0\leq t<588\) gives
\[
 2^{t+2}-(t+2)\equiv49\pmod{196}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 t\in\{181,413,429\}. \tag{7}
\]
This calculation is a simple recurrence: begin with \(2^2\bmod196\), double modulo \(196\) as \(t\) increases by one, subtract \(t+2\), and compare with \(49\). Thus (6) forces
\[
 (k-2)\bmod588\in\{181,413,429\}. \tag{8}
\]

Next write the Euclidean division of \(k-2\) by \(29400\) as
\[
 k=j+2+29400q,
 \qquad 0\leq j<29400. \tag{9}
\]
Because \(29400=50\cdot588\), condition (8) becomes
\[
 j\bmod588\in\{181,413,429\}. \tag{10}
\]
There are only \(50\cdot3=150\) values of \(j\) in the indicated range satisfying (10).

For such a \(j\), let \(P_j\) be the least nonnegative residue of \(2^{j+2}\) modulo \(N\), and define
\[
 b_j\equiv P_j-(j+2+63945)\pmod N,
 \qquad 0\leq b_j<N. \tag{11}
\]
By (4) and (9), congruence (5) is equivalent to
\[
 b_j\equiv29400q\pmod{550172}. \tag{12}
\]
Now
\[
 \gcd(29400,550172)=196,
 \qquad \frac{29400}{196}=150,
 \qquad \frac{550172}{196}=2807.
\]
Condition (10), together with (7), also shows directly that \(b_j\) is divisible by \(196\). Dividing (12) by \(196\) therefore gives
\[
 150q\equiv b_j/196\pmod{2807}. \tag{13}
\]
The inverse of \(150\) modulo \(2807\) is \(131\), since
\[
 150\cdot131=19650=7\cdot2807+1.
\]
Consequently (13) forces
\[
 q\equiv Q_j:=131(b_j/196)\pmod{2807}, \tag{14}
\]
where \(Q_j\) is chosen in \(0\leq Q_j<2807\).

On the other hand, the assumed upper bound on \(k\) in (5), together with (9), implies \(q\leq570<2807\). Hence the congruence (14) is not merely a congruence: it forces
\[
 q=Q_j. \tag{15}
\]

It remains only to perform the finite calculation for the 150 possible values of \(j\) specified by (10). For each one, compute \(P_j=2^{j+2}\bmod550172\) by repeated squaring, form \(b_j\) by (11), and then form
\[
 Q_j=(131(b_j/196))\bmod2807.
\]
The resulting calculation gives
\[
 j+2+29400Q_j\geq17135927
 \quad\text{for every one of the 150 possible }j. \tag{16}
\]
The minimum is attained at
\[
 j=25125,\qquad Q_j=582,
\]
for which
\[
 25125+2+29400\cdot582=17135927.
\]
In particular every value in (16) is greater than
\(2^{24}=16777216\). Equations (9) and (15) therefore contradict the bound on \(k\) in (5). We have proved
\[
 2^k-k\not\equiv63945\pmod{550172}
 \quad\text{for every }1\leq k<16777216. \tag{17}
\]

For completeness, we also establish that \(a(550172)\) really is defined: every residue modulo \(550172\) eventually occurs. This follows from the same period and a small table modulo \(196\).

For each \(u=0,1,\ldots,195\), choose \(s(u)\) from the following list, whose entries are in order of increasing \(u\):
\[
\begin{split}
[&36,143,2,349,308,3,26,225,332,191,50,81,4,31,58,85,48,139,98,193,\\
&220,15,122,237,328,287,146,5,204,311,170,29,60,171,10,37,64,27,118,77,\\
&172,199,226,101,216,307,266,125,72,183,290,149,8,39,150,173,16,43,6,97,\\
&56,151,178,205,80,195,286,245,104,51,162,269,128,475,18,129,152,11,22,49,\\
&76,35,130,157,184,59,174,265,224,83,30,141,248,107,454,413,108,131,330,437,\\
&28,55,14,109,136,163,38,153,244,203,62,9,120,227,86,433,392,87,110,309,416,7,\\
&34,61,88,115,142,17,132,223,182,41,304,99,206,65,412,371,66,89,288,395,254,13,\\
&40,67,94,121,148,111,202,161,20,283,78,185,44,391,350,45,68,267,374,233,12,19,\\
&46,73,100,127,90,181,140,235,262,57,164,23,370,329,24,47,246,353,212,71,102,25,\\
&52,79,106,69,160,119,214,241].
\end{split}
\]
A direct modular calculation gives, for every \(u\),
\[
 2\leq s(u)<29400,
 \qquad 2^{s(u)}-s(u)\equiv u\pmod{196}. \tag{18}
\]
The largest table entry is only \(475\), and (18) is checked by repeated doubling modulo \(196\).

Let \(r\) be any integer with \(0\leq r<N\), and take
\[
 s=s(r\bmod196).
\]
By (18),
\[
 2^s-s\equiv r\pmod{196},

a fact equivalently written as
\[
 s\equiv2^s+N-r\pmod{196}. \tag{19}
\]
Because \(196=\gcd(29400,N)\), the generalized Chinese remainder theorem says that the simultaneous congruences
\[
 x\equiv s\pmod{29400},
 \qquad x\equiv2^s+N-r\pmod N \tag{20}
\]
have a solution precisely when their right sides agree modulo \(196\). That compatibility is exactly (19), so choose a nonnegative solution \(x\).

Since \(0<s<29400\), the first congruence in (20) lets us write
\[
 x=s+29400q
\]
for some \(q\geq0\); in particular \(x\geq s\geq2\). Using (2) and the periodicity principle,
\[
 2^x=2^{s+29400q}\equiv2^s\pmod N.
\]
The second congruence in (20) says
\[
 x\equiv2^s-r\pmod N.
\]
Subtracting, we obtain
\[
 2^x-x\equiv r\pmod N.
\]
Thus every residue \(r\) modulo \(N\) occurs for some positive exponent. Since there are only finitely many residues, taking the maximum of one chosen exponent for each residue produces an \(m\) for which \(f(1),\ldots,f(m)\) cover all residues. Hence \(a(N)\) exists and, by its definition as the least such \(m\), its initial segment really does cover every residue modulo \(N\).

It remains to compare the conjectured bound with \(2^{24}\). A finite prime sieve gives
\[
 \pi(8216744)=553390. \tag{21}
\]
Here the sieve starts with the integers below \(8216744\), removes the multiples \(p^2,p^2+p,\ldots\) for each still-unremoved \(p\leq\sqrt{8216743}\), and counts the remaining integers. Every removed integer is composite, and every composite below the endpoint has a prime factor at most its square root, so the remaining integers are exactly the primes. This explains both the mathematical validity and the finite reproducibility of (21). In particular, since
\[
 553390>550172
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 8216744<8388608=2^{23},
\]
the \(550172\)-nd prime satisfies
\[
 p_{550172}<2^{23}. \tag{22}
\]
(Indeed, a full sieve locates it at \(8165753\), though that sharper value is unnecessary.)

Assume now that the conjecture were true for every positive \(n\). Applying it to \(N=550172\), and using (22), would give
\[
 a(N)<2(p_N-1)<2\cdot2^{23}=2^{24}. \tag{23}
\]
By the defining covering property of \(a(N)\), the residue \(63945\) would then equal \(2^k-k\pmod N\) for some
\[
 1\leq k\leq a(N)<2^{24}.
\]
This contradicts (17). Therefore the asserted inequality fails at
\[
 \boxed{n=550172},
\]
and the conjecture “\(a(n)<2(p_n-1)\) for every \(n>0\)” is false.
